preamble: Under the laryngeal theory, the Proto-Indo-European laryngeal *h₃ became the vowel o in Greek when it had to carry a syllable: between consonants (*dh₃tós > δοτός) and word-initially before a consonant, where it surfaces as a 'prothetic' vowel (*h₃negʰ- > ὄνυξ). The atlas symbol [h] stands in for *h₃, whose phonetic value is reconstructed as a rounded fricative (perhaps [ɣʷ] or [ʕʷ]) rather than a glottal [h]. This vocalization is distinct from laryngeal colouring, in which *h₃ next to *e turned the vowel into o and was itself lost; colouring does not belong in this cell. Only Greek keeps an o reflex: Latin, Germanic and Celtic give a (see h_to_a), Indo-Iranian i (see h_to_i).

examples.note: Zero grade of *deh₃- 'give'; interconsonantal *h₃ vocalized to o. Compare θετός (*dʰh₁tós, e) and στατός (*sth₂tós, a), the Greek triple reflex.
Word-initial *h₃ before a consonant gives the prothetic vowel o-; Latin unguis and Sanskrit nakhá- show no such vowel.
Prothetic o- again; compare Sanskrit mehati and Latin mingō.
Prothetic o- before the consonant; compare Latin dēns and Sanskrit dánt-.
